To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
manual therapy and exercise appear to provide a better short-term outcome for acute neck pain than do other treatments.

for neck pain without radiculopathy, there is evidence to support the use of manual therapy, therapeutic exercise, and manipulation for patients with neck-related arm pain, and there is fair evidence to support the inclusion of education, advice to remain active, and advice to perform exercises.

for patients with neck disorders without radicular symptoms: (1) manual and supervised exercise therapies are more effective than other interventions in the short term and (2) manual and supervised exercises, low level laser, and acupuncture are more effective in the short term than no treatment, placebo or alternative interventions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of neck pain and its related disorders, including whiplash associated disorder.
the treatment of neck pain, and in particular the treatment of neck disorders in which there is no evidence of radicular symptoms.
the development of a novel approach to the design of a novel approach.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for both whiplash and neck pain without radiculopathy, manual therapy and exercise appear to be the most effective interventions, and for whiplash, education is also important.
for neck pain, manual therapy and exercises are more effective than other noninvasive interventions.
there is evidence that manual therapy and exercise interventions are effective in the short- and long-term management of neck pain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evidence for the effectiveness of noninvasive treatments is generally weak, and the quality of the evidence is generally poor.

manual therapy and exercise is more effective than alternative interventions for neck pain, and therapies that focus on regaining function are relatively more effective for patients with whiplash associated neck pain.
there is a paucity of high quality evidence for most noninvasive interventions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have identified a number of interventions for patients with neck disorders that have some evidence of effectiveness and are relatively safe.
there is no one treatment that is superior to another.
there is a lack of good evidence to guide the treatment of neck pain.
